title: I have seen thy tears (2 Kings 20:1–6)
hook: told he will die, Hezekiah turns to the wall and weeps, and is given fifteen years
carry: the weeping was part of the prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hezekiah spread a threatening letter before God. Your line was lay it open before you answer. Today, the same king gets news no letter could match.

Set your house in order, "for thou shalt die, and not live." That's what the prophet Isaiah says at the bedside of King Hezekiah, who is sick, the text says, unto death. No softening. No second opinion. It comes from the prophet himself, in the name of God. Some news closes a door so firmly that there seems nothing left to say. What Hezekiah does next is a small movement of the body you can almost see.
screen: `SICK UNTO DEATH.` → `SET YOUR HOUSE IN ORDER.` → `WHAT IS LEFT TO SAY?`

segments.voice: He turns his face to the wall, away from the room, with the prophet still standing there. And he prays, short and honest: remember now how I have walked before you in truth and with a whole heart, and done what is good in your sight. Then the text adds: Hezekiah wept sore. Now watch the speed of what follows. Before Isaiah has even made it out of the courtyard, the word of the Lord comes to him: turn back. Tell Hezekiah, "I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears". I will heal you. On the third day you'll go up to the house of the Lord, and I will add to your days fifteen years. Notice the pair: heard and seen. God hears the words and also sees the tears. The weeping isn't treated as weakness or a failure of faith. It is part of the prayer, the part that gets seen. The Talmud tells a version of this scene in which Hezekiah answers Isaiah with a teaching from his ancestors' house: even when a sharp sword rests on a person's neck, they should not hold back from asking for mercy. The verdict sounded final. He prayed anyway. Why did the decree change? The text doesn't explain, and readers have argued about it. What it does make plain is the picture: a man facing the wall, crying, and a God who notices the tears.
screen: `HE TURNED HIS FACE TO THE WALL.` · `HEZEKIAH WEPT SORE.` · then, large: `HEARD THY PRAYER, SEEN THY TEARS.` · then: `A SWORD ON THE NECK, STILL ASK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind some news that felt like a closed door, a diagnosis, a rejection, a no, and if it helps, turn slightly away from the room, the way Hezekiah turned to the wall. Say silently what's true, what you've tried and what you hope, and if tears come, let them; they're allowed here. If you pray, you can ask for mercy even now; if you don't, just speak honestly, even after the news.
Isaiah, the prophet who told Hezekiah to set his house in order, then returned to say, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears.
Your line: the weeping was part of the prayer. Heard and seen, both. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jews read Hezekiah's illness in the book of Kings and again in Isaiah 38, and the Talmud draws from it the teaching that a person keeps asking for mercy even when things look hopeless.

chat.says: Isn't crying when you pray a sign your faith is weak?
options: In Hezekiah's story God says, I have seen thy tears. Weeping is part of prayer.
Yes, the story praises Hezekiah for holding back his tears before God.
Tears don't matter there; God only answers the words that are said.
chat.meaning: God sends Isaiah back to say: I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears. The weeping isn't weakness; it's part of what is seen.
